addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per
commit that lands on the branch, so reading it top to bottom
is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are
the program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the anticipated close-out
titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may
split into two cycles). `docs:` entries are interludes that
sit between cycles and belong to no rung. Every shipped ref
points at a close-out commit on `refactor-vc-x1`, treated as
permanent: the branch is long-lived and lands on main
merge-only, never rebased.

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.4. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

108	- [[N]] 0.78.0-3 feat: jj-lib version gate
109	  - our side is compile-time by nature, not by compromise:
110	    the linked jj-lib is what writes ops. A `build.rs` reads
111	    the resolved version out of `Cargo.lock` and exports
112	    `JJ_LIB_VERSION` via `cargo::rustc-env`, with
113	    `rerun-if-changed` on the lock.
114	  - read `$CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/Cargo.lock` directly rather
115	    than walking ancestors: we are not a workspace, and a
116	    walk can bind a sibling project's lock, which is worse
117	    than failing
118	  - their side is `jj -V`, printing `jj 0.43.0-<hash>`, so
119	    compare the triple by prefix match or regex, never whole
120	    string equality
121	  - a version stamp in the repo data would beat asking the
122	    binary, but the one that exists is the wrong one: the
123	    index carries a format version, and it is self-healing
124	    derived data whose constant is `pub(super)`, while the
125	    op store, the thing we would be co-writing, carries none
126	  - rests on jj-cli and jj-lib releasing in lockstep; verify
127	    against the jj-cli manifest and record the assumption,
128	    since equality becomes the wrong test if they diverge
129	  - refuse on the write path only, with an explicit override
130	    flag, so a jj upgrade never blocks a read
131	  - the `.vc-config.toml` pin turns a `$PATH` sample into a
132	    declaration, but only matters once more than one jj is in
133	    play; it stays a Todo
134	- [[N]] 0.78.0-4 refactor: jj-lib mutations
135	  - commit, describe, bookmark set/track, fetch, push, plus
136	    the `@`-relative reads deferred from `-2`
137	- [[N]] 0.78.0-5 fix: jj-lib index-lock retry
138	  - bugs.md #1, with the `git init --bare` to gix rider
139	  - the retry classifies by error variant rather than
140	    substring, which is the real win: `SpawnInPath` and
141	    `UnsupportedGitOption` are never retryable, and treating
142	    the whole `Subprocess` arm as retryable would loop
143	    forever on a missing git binary
144	- [[N]] 0.78.0 refactor: jj-lib migration (close-out)
145	
146	##### Decisions at cycle open
147	
148	- **All three pieces**, decided 2026-07-30: jj-lib for reads,
149	  jj-lib for mutations, and the index-lock retry that is the
150	  headline prize. The 2026-07-29 session ended undecided
151	  between this and deferring mutations.
152	- **What changed is the coexistence objection, not the
153	  evidence.** The risk section concluded the coupling was
154	  "unenforceable, probably fine" because a `jj --version`
155	  check cannot answer whether two versions are compatible.
156	  That evaluates it as a compatibility oracle. As a guard on
157	  our own writes it fits the actual risk direction: the
158	  dangerous case is an old jj reading an op written by a
159	  newer jj-lib, and refusing to write on a mismatch closes
160	  exactly that. The safe direction, a newer jj reading our
161	  older op, is something jj must support anyway, since the
162	  user's own older jj wrote into that repo first.
163	- **The gate lands at `-3`, before the mutations at `-4`**, so
164	  mutations arrive in a repo that already refuses on
165	  mismatch. The cost is one commit whose check guards nothing
166	  yet, which reads oddly in isolation; folding it into `-4`
167	  would avoid that but make one rung do two things.

content.text:
Enough reading; here are my thoughts on both tasks. No changes made.

## 1. Review of `-0` and the cycle plan

The `-0` commit itself looks right: cycle block moved (not copied) into `## In Progress`, `fix-todo` renumber, the `Commits:` backfill for 0.77.4, version bumped to `0.78.0-0`, ochid trailer present, and the body follows the file-by-file form. The one-home note (narrative in TODO.md, chores receives it at close-out) matches the 0.77.0-2 convention. No repair needed there.

On the plan, three points, two of which I'd want to change in TODO.md (with your approval):

1. **Mismatch direction at `-3` is underspecified.** The decisions block correctly identifies the risk as one-directional: dangerous is old jj reading ops written by a newer jj-lib; the reverse is something jj must support anyway. But the ladder bullet says refuse "on a mismatch", which reads as any inequality. If installed jj is *newer* than our jj-lib, refusing buys nothing and blocks users who upgraded jj before we bumped the dependency — the exact safe direction the decisions block blesses. I'd amend the `-3` bullet to: refuse only when jj-lib's version is newer than the installed jj; equal or older proceeds. This also affects what `-1` documents, so it's worth settling now.

2. **`-3` doesn't say what happens when `jj` isn't on `$PATH`.** The gate samples `jj -V`; a machine without a jj binary can't answer. My lean: proceed with a warning (no jj binary means no old jj on this machine to misread our ops, and the override flag exists), but whichever way you want it, the bullet should say. Related edge: `jj-lib 0.43.0` vs `jj 0.43.0-<hash>` prerelease/dev builds — the prefix-match bullet covers it, fine.

3. **Minor, no change needed:** the `(current)` markers (program rung `0.78.0` and sub-rung `-0`) are stale-but-correct per convention — they advance as part of the next commit's edits. And the read/write split at `-2` (deferring `@`-relative reads because snapshotting is an op-store write) is the right cut; I have nothing to add to it.

If you approve points 1 and 2, the edits are a few lines in the `-3` bullet block; they'd ride into `-1` naturally since `-1` is the docs rung recording this exact policy — so one option is to fold them into `-1`'s work rather than touching TODO.md before it.

## 2. Universal AGENTS.md

The drift numbers tell the story: the template keeps `AGENTS-vc-x1.md` within 19 lines of ours, but the "generic" template AGENTS.md is 429 lines away, iiac-perf 442, zc-ring-x1 582. There is no shared core anymore — there are four ~800-line forks, and a fix learned in one repo never propagates. That's the maintenance half of the problem. The adherence half is different, and worth being honest about:

**Why I fail to follow the current files.** It's almost never disagreement; it's recall at the moment of action. The rules that get broken (pre-committing a rung, the hard stop after push, dropped trailers, title identity, punctuation) are procedural constraints buried in ~1,800 lines across AGENTS.md + cycle-protocol.md + satellites, written as narrative-with-rationale. Rationale is what makes the rules *right*, but at decision time I need the imperative, and extracting it from prose under a full working context is where slips happen. Length itself is a cost: everything always-loaded competes for attention with the actual task.

So the redesign should optimize for two distinct readers: the agent *about to act* (needs a short checklist) and the agent *asking why* (needs the rationale). Today one document serves both and serves the first badly.

**Proposed shape:**

- **`AGENTS.md`** (universal, short — I'd aim for 150–250 lines): the dual-repo model, the invariants that must never be violated (a numbered hard-rules list: push commits the rung, never pre-commit; hard stop after push; never re-describe published; trailers are push's job; ...), and a map of the satellite files. Byte-identical across every repo — that's the enforcement mechanism: `diff` against the template must come back empty, so drift is detectable mechanically, and `vc-x1` could grow a `validate-agents` that checks it.
- **Satellite topic files** in a directory — your `./agent-data/` works; I'd bikeshed toward `agents/` for brevity, but the name matters less than the split: `cycle.md` (protocol + checklists), `prose.md` (prose form, punctuation, anchors, references), `notes.md` (todo/chores/done mechanics), `jj.md` (jj basics + ochid), `code.md` (per-medium conventions). These absorb most of today's AGENTS.md plus cycle-protocol.md. Also universal, also diff-enforced.
- **Checklists as first-class content.** Each procedural moment gets a ≤10-line imperative checklist (`Before push:`, `Per work commit:`, `At close-out:`) placed at the *top* of its topic file, rationale below. Rule first, why after — inverting today's order. This is the single change I'd bet most improves adherence, because a checklist can be re-read in full right before the action.
- **`custom.md`** — your idea, and I think it's the right one. One file per repo that is the *only* file agents may modify; it's loaded last and wins conflicts. It holds what genuinely varies: project structure, the medium's validation cycle (cargo vs. prose vs. whatever), versioning specifics, project-local rules like iiac-perf's extras. The "only place" contract becomes checkable for free once the universal files are diff-pinned: any edit outside `custom.md` shows up as template drift. I'd also give `custom.md` a stated schema — named override points ("validation command:", "extra hard rules:") rather than freeform — so customizations stay greppable across repos.
- **Template repo as source of truth.** `vc-x1-work-repo-template` stops carrying per-project forks (`AGENTS-vc-x1.md`, `AGENTS-iiac-perf.md` die); those become each repo's `custom.md`. Propagating a rule fix = copying the universal files, which is now safe because nothing project-specific lives in them.

One caution: the current files encode real hard-won detail (trapezoid recipe, ochid resolvability, anchor slugging). Universalizing must not mean discarding it — it means relocating it under the topic files with the checklists in front. And some of today's content is genuinely vc-x1-project history ("hit at the 0.77.2 amend") that belongs in `notes/`, not in the universal rules at all; the rewrite is a chance to sort rule from record.

The plain version: the instructions grew into four different long books, and I keep fumbling not because the rules are wrong but because the important ones are buried in explanation. Make one short shared rulebook identical everywhere, move the explanations into a few side files, put short do-this-now checklists where the mistakes actually happen, and give each project exactly one file where its differences live.

Both tasks await your call: approve/adjust the two `-3` plan amendments (and whether they land now or fold into `-1`), and whether this AGENTS.md shape is worth drafting.

content.text:
Thoughts on both tweaks:

## Strict gate: `ver-A != ver-B` → stop

Agreed, and I'll withdraw my direction-aware refinement as the *starting* policy — it becomes the documented loosening path instead. Fail-closed-then-loosen is the right order because the two errors aren't symmetric: starting strict costs friction we can observe and relax; starting loose risks an op-store incident we'd learn about from a corrupted repo. A few consequences worth capturing when `-1`/`-3` land:

- "Equality" should mean **triple equality**, not string equality — `jj -V` prints `jj 0.43.0-<hash>`, so we compare `0.43.0` against jj-lib's resolved version and ignore the suffix. Otherwise the gate can never pass.
- The strict gate **will trip routinely**: jj releases roughly monthly, and every user-side jj upgrade blocks writes until we bump jj-lib (or they override). That's not a flaw, it's the experiment — each trip is a data point in exactly the safe direction (jj newer than jj-lib), which is the evidence base for loosening later. The error message should carry both versions and name the override flag, so a trip costs seconds, not a debugging session.
- The missing-binary case gets the consistent strict answer: **no `jj` on `$PATH` → stop too** (can't verify, so refuse), override available. One rule, no special cases.
- `-1` records the policy as: strict equality now; the direction-aware relaxation (refuse only when jj-lib is newer than jj) is the anticipated loosening, with the risk asymmetry as its justification, once trips confirm the safe direction is the common one.

On where these plan amendments land, my earlier suggestion stands: fold them into `-1`'s work (it's the docs rung recording this exact policy) with the small `-3` bullet touch-up riding on that same commit, rather than a separate TODO.md edit now. Say the word and that's the plan of record for `-1`.

## Template as discussion venue, and the proposal files

Good correction — I read the `AGENTS-xxx` files as drift-forks to kill; as a central place where multiple agents park their copies to discuss, they make sense, and the proposal slots right into that convention. `AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730.md` reads as `<repo>-<author-model>-<date>`, which future responding agents can mirror (`AGENTS-iiac-perf-<model>-<date>.md`), so the discussion stays one file per voice, diffable and committed.

On the split between the draft and its companion:

- **`AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730.md`**: the proposed universal AGENTS.md *as it would ship* — clean, no meta-commentary, so it can be diffed against the current files and eventually copied verbatim. The hard-rules list and the file map are its core.
- **The companion** (I'd name it `AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730-notes.md`, same stem so they sort together): everything that shouldn't ship — the adherence analysis (recall-at-moment-of-action, not disagreement), the checklist-first inversion and its rationale, the `custom.md` contract and precedence, the diff-pinning enforcement idea, a migration sketch, and an explicit **open questions** section for other agents to answer.
- **Satellite files stay sketched, not drafted, in round one.** The full `agents/` (or `agent-data/`) tree is five-plus files; drafting them before the shape is agreed multiplies review cost and anchors the discussion on wording instead of structure. The companion should carry each satellite's proposed table of contents plus the *checklists in full* — the checklists are the highest-value content to get eyes on early, and they're short enough to review as a block.

One process thought: the companion's open-questions section should include the ones I can't settle alone — the directory name, whether `custom.md` gets a fixed schema of named override points or stays freeform, and whether cycle-protocol.md merges into the satellite tree or stays a `notes/` file that the tree points at. Those are the forks where other repos' experience genuinely differs from vc-x1's.

The plain version: start the version check as "must match exactly, otherwise stop, with an escape hatch," and only relax it after we've seen how often and in which direction it actually fires. For the proposal, write two files: the rulebook exactly as it would be adopted, and a separate discussion file explaining the reasoning and listing the questions other agents should weigh in on.

Awaiting your go: (a) confirm the `-1` fold-in as the plan of record, and (b) green-light drafting the two proposal files in `../vc-x1-work-repo-template/`.

content.text:
Dogfooding it is the right call — a rulebook whose whole thesis is "adherence fails at the moment of action" can only be validated by an agent actually running on it, and 0.78.0 is a good testbed: the cycle has docs rungs, refactor rungs, riders, and a trapezoid close-out ahead, so most checklists get exercised for real. Thoughts on what the tweak changes:

**Authority flips during the dogfood window, and we should say so explicitly.** My earlier "template is source of truth, diff-pinned" model now applies only *after* promotion. During 0.78.0: vc-x1's local copy is the working draft and gets amended freely as experience dictates; the template's `AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730.md` is a frozen, dated proposal snapshot for discussion — not synced, not authoritative. The dated filename carries that meaning nicely. Promotion to the template (en masse or incremental, as you said) is the moment diff-pinning switches on and the flow reverses. Being explicit about this avoids re-creating the drift problem inside the project meant to solve it.

**Adoption needs a rung, and it can't stay a sketch.** Two consequences for the plan:

- Running on the new AGENTS means vc-x1 needs the *complete working tree* — main file, satellites, `custom.md` — not just the main-plus-sketches I proposed for review round one. So the drafting scope grows: full tree drafted for local adoption; the template still receives just the two discussion files (draft main + companion with satellite ToCs and full checklists), as the snapshot other agents review.
- The ladder needs a slot. Adoption is a sizable notes-only change that shouldn't ride on `-1` (version-coupling policy — mixing in an AGENTS rewrite makes one rung do two unrelated things, against the very rules being adopted). I'd insert it as the new `0.78.0-1 docs: adopt universal AGENTS` and shift the rest down one; unshipped rung versions are explicitly provisional in TODO.md, so the renumber is sanctioned. It should land *before* the coupling-policy rung so the remaining five commits all run under the new rules — maximum dogfood coverage.

**Reorganize first, don't re-legislate.** For the v1 draft I'd hold rule *semantics* fixed and change only structure: same rules, new shape (short main, checklists first, rationale in satellites, project specifics in `custom.md`). If we change organization and content at once, we can't attribute any adherence improvement to the structure — and the structure is the hypothesis under test. Semantic changes we discover we want become dogfood findings, not v1 edits.

**Amendments are the data; log them.** Mid-cycle, small rule fixes ride as riders on whatever rung is in flight (noted in the commit body), big ones get their own docs rung. Either way, each amendment gets a one-line entry in a local dogfood log — which rule failed or chafed, and what changed — because that log *is* the evidence for the promotion decision, exactly parallel to the version gate's "every trip is a data point." Natural home: a section in `custom.md` or a small `notes/` file; slight lean toward `custom.md` since it's already the designated mutable surface.

**One continuity note:** `-0` was authored under the old rules and the rest of the cycle under the new; since v1 is reorganization-only, the records (chores shape, title identity, trailer handling) stay compatible and the cycle's paper trail remains coherent. That's another reason to keep semantics fixed in v1.

The plain version: we'll write the new rulebook in full, start living by it in this repo for the rest of this cycle, and keep notes on every place it pinches. The copy in the shared template is a dated snapshot for other agents to discuss, not the live version. When the local copy has proven itself, it moves to the template and becomes the standard everyone copies.

Awaiting your go on the consolidated plan: (a) fold the gate-policy amendments into the coupling-policy rung as agreed; (b) insert `docs: adopt universal AGENTS` as the new `-1`, renumbering the rest; (c) draft the full tree locally + the two dated proposal files in the template, semantics-preserving.

content.content:
1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
7	the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
8	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
9	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
10	equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
11	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
12	
13	## Cycles
14	
15	A cycle has three phases:
16	
17	- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`): the cycle's
18	  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
19	  it and starts at `-1`; see
20	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
21	  cycle:
22	  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
23	    and the suffix scheme are project-specific; see
24	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
25	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
26	    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
27	    statement + plan ladder).
28	  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
29	- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...): the
30	  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
31	  needs; each runs through the
32	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
33	- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`): the cycle's
34	  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
35	  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
36	    `## Done`.
37	  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
38	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
39	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
40	    changed.
41	
42	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
43	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
44	result must always be published at close-out. See
45	[Pushing](#pushing).
46	
47	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
48	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides: `X.Y.Z-3.0`
49	Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
50	Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
51	at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
52	suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
53	for the local-ladder mechanics.
54	
55	## Chores sections
56	
57	A **chores section** is a `##` section in
58	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
59	general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
60	should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
61	chores file.
62	
63	The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
64	`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
65	with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
66	followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
67	then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
68	lands**, so the chores record is built up per commit, not held
69	back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
70	*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
71	`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
72	later, once the commit is permanent (see
73	[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
74	
75	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
76	design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
77	AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).
78	
79	### Commits backfill
80	
81	A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
82	records, by SHA, but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
83	lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
84	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
85	squash rewrites it on the way. So:
86	
87	- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
88	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
89	  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
90	  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
91	  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
92	  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
93	  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands,
94	  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
95	  invalidate.
96	
97	Use `[[N]]` refs, several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
98	section records multiple commits (a push that publishes
99	several), with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's
100	`# References`
101	(format in AGENTS.md
102	[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
103	A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
104	deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
105	`git log --grep "<title>"`.
106	
107	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma. A
108	**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
109	close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
110	SHA must be permanent.
111	
112	## Preparation
113	
114	The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
115	setup (a lightweight cycle omits it; see
116	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):
117	
118	- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
119	  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
120	  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
121	  project-specific; see [versioning.md](versioning.md).
122	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
123	  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:
124	  - A **bold title line**, which will be the chores
125	    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.
126	  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed
127	  - A **plan ladder**.
128	- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)**: append a
129	  `##` header with the title it records, the cycle's
130	  anticipated close-out title.
131	
132	## Work-N
133	
134	The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
135	implement the change. As many as needed:
136	
137	- Each commit runs through the
138	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
139	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
140	  visibility).
141	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
142	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
143	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
144	  scope grows enough (see
145	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
146	
147	## Close-out
148	
149	The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping
150	only, and the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not
151	what happens post-squash:
152	
153	- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
154	  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
155	- **Finalize the chores section** (opened during Preparation
156	  and grown per commit; see [Chores sections](#chores-sections)):
157	  - The problem statement is already the chores intro (written
158	    when the section was opened) and the plan ladder is already
159	    the `### As-built ladder` (a rung appended per commit), so
160	    close-out only *finalizes*, it does not cut-and-paste.
161	  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title if the
162	    cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor back-reference.
163	  - Add any `### design subsections`; optional `### Outcome`
164	    notes.
165	  - Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block with
166	    `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a multi-cycle
167	    program (program `###`, current stage `####`) this retires
168	    the stage `####` only; the program heading and its ladder
169	    stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`, so the marker
170	    sits inside the program block until the next stage is
171	    picked up.
172	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
173	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
174	
175	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
176	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time; see
177	[Pushing](#pushing).
178	
179	## Numbering
180	
181	Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix: `-0`
182	Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/... Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
183	recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme (disambiguation,
184	nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
185	format, and the per-phase bump) lives in
186	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
187	single source of truth for this repo's versioning.
188	
189	## Per-commit flow
190	
191	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
192	through:
193	
194	1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
195	   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
196	   root).
197	2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
198	   for the loop-and-squash technique).
199	3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
200	   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
201	4. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
202	   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
203	   example the cargo cycle is:
204	   1. `cargo fmt`
205	   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
206	   3. `cargo test`
207	   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
208	   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
209	5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
210	   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
211	   changes and we iterate until complete.
212	6. **Write the commit description**; see
213	   [Commit description](#commit-description).
214	7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
215	   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
216	8. **Commit + push.** Hand the approved title/body to
217	   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`, whose
218	   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
219	   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
220	   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate
221	   (bugs.md #6). Push approval is per-push, so step 7's
222	   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
223	   includes the push.
224	
225	**Two overrides apply:**
226	
227	- **Deviation or question.** Any time the work deviates
228	  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
229	  surface it; don't push through.
230	- **ESC-ESC.** The user can interrupt at any point to pull
231	  a review or question forward.
232	
233	## Commit description
234	
235	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
236	
237	```
238	<type>: <short description>
239	```
240	
241	Titles carry **no trailing `(<version>)` suffix**. The
242	version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
243	[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming
244	you're running the version you're testing, not a per-commit
245	title marker. We think per-commit version-in-title is
246	unstable on large projects: many changes are in flight
247	simultaneously, and a version is only stable once merged into
248	the main repo, so titles don't carry one.
249	
250	### Title
251	
252	- ≤50 chars total.
253	- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
254	  `docs`, `chore`.
255	- Favor terse phrasings.
256	- **Distinct per step.** Each of a cycle's commits gets its
257	  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
258	  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
259	  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the
260	  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
261	  AGENTS.md
262	  [Conventional-commit shape](../AGENTS.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
263	
264	### Body
265	
266	[Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),
267	wrap ≤72. Bullet content differs per repo:
268	
269	- **Work-repo body**: file-by-file. One bullet per file
270	  changed (file plus a one-line gist). Sub-bullets for
271	  files with multiple distinct changes:
272	
273	  ```
274	  - path/to/file1
275	    - first distinct change
276	    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line
277	       with continuation indented 5
278	  ```
279	
280	  The list **opens with the version bump** as its first
281	  bullet, for the Rust example
282	  `- Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock: version X.Y.Z-N` (generally:
283	  the medium's version-of-record files). Titles stay
284	  version-free (above), so this first bullet is the
285	  version's durable, visible home, and log viewers (e.g.
286	  gitk's message pane) show it without opening the commit's
287	  file list. Adopted 2026-07-24.
288	
289	  The file-by-file list is the source of truth for the
290	  cycle's mechanical change record. Chores carries the
291	  narrative + design, not a copy of it. Promote any
292	  "why" beyond one sentence to a chores `###` subsection.
293	
294	- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe
295	  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.
296	
297	### Trailer
298	
299	`ochid:` as the last line of the body; see
300	[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](../AGENTS.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
301	in AGENTS.md for the convention.
302	
303	For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
304	trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
305	space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
306	hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.
307	
308	## Reviewing changes
309	
310	Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
311	on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
312	editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:
313	
314	- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
315	- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
316	- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
317	- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev
318	
319	Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
320	it mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or
321	`jj show -r @-`.
322	
323	See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
324	close-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives
325	are in [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets).
326	
327	## Pushing
328	
329	### Policy
330	
331	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
332	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
333	the cycle's result must be published.
334	
335	**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
336	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
337	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
338	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
339	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
340	the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
341	
342	**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
343	the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
344	commit-description review that shows title+body and stops, and
345	the hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
346	default*.
347	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
348	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
349	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
350	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
351	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
352	
353	- **Explicit grant.** Never inferred from a task merely being
354	  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
355	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
356	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
357	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
358	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
359	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
360	  unattended") waives them.
361	- **Bounded goal.** Covers the named task only; does not carry
362	  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
363	- **Destructive ops still pause.** Delegation covers the task's
364	  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
365	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
366	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
367	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
368	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
369	  reaches this.
370	- **Still transparent.** Report each commit/push as it lands
371	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
372	- **When in doubt, ask.** Ambiguous authorization falls back to
373	  per-push approval.
374	
375	### Shape at close-out push
376	
377	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
378	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
379	the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
380	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
381	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
382	
383	- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
384	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
385	  focused on one or two files.
386	- **Trapezoid** (a `git merge --no-ff` merge commit)
387	  *(current default)*: the target gains a merge commit
388	  (`X.Y.Z`) whose first parent is the trunk line and whose
389	  second parent is the cycle's ladder, so
390	  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while
391	  every rung stays reachable. See
392	  [Trapezoid close-out recipe](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
393	  for the full sequence.
394	- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
395	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
396	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
397	  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.
398	
399	A squash is set up before invoking `vc-x1 push`; a trapezoid
400	is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
401	other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.
402	
403	### Trapezoid close-out recipe
404	
405	A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
406	published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
407	two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
408	bookmark at the reshaped commit.
409	
410	```
411	  main line   ...──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
412	                      \                    /
413	  ladder             <rung-1>──...──<tip>─┘
414	```
415	
416	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
417	  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
418	  first parent.
419	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
420	  second parent.
421	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.
422	
423	The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
424	because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
425	remains is reshaping and publishing them:
426	
427	1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
428	   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
429	   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
430	2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
431	   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
432	   argument order.
433	3. `jj new <closeout>`
434	   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
435	4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
436	   - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
437	   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
438	   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
439	   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.
440	
441	**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
442	close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
443	none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
444	time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
445	from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
446	stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
447	requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
448	but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
449	different operation from committing and publishing, and only
450	the latter is push's job.
451	
452	#### Details
453	
454	- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
455	  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
456	  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
457	  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
458	  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
459	  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
460	  once published.
461	- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
462	  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
463	  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
464	  rung, not the last close-out.
465	- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
466	  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
467	  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
468	  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
469	  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
470	  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
471	  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
472	  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
473	  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
474	  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
475	- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
476	  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
477	  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
478	  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
479	- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
480	  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
481	  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
482	  [`Commits:` backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
483	  SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
484	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
485	  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
486	  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
487	  push force-updates the target.
488	- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
489	  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
490	  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
491	  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
492	  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
493	
494	#### Recovery
495	
496	- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
497	  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
498	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
499	  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
500	  Do not push a shape you did not intend; after step 4 the
501	  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
502	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
503	  `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
504	  affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
505	  made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
506	  rebase onto the merge.
507	- **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
508	  `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
509	  If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
510	  sideways move, not a rewrite.
511	
512	### vc-x1 push wrapper
513	
514	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
515	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
516	work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
517	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
518	
519	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
520	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
521	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
522	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`;
523	this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
524	
525	### .claude cadence
526	
527	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
528	with every work-repo commit in that push.
529	
530	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
531	across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
532	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
533	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
534	
535	`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
536	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
537	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
538	work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
539	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
540	
541	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
542	session information created, which we don't worry about.
543	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
544	remain empty.
545	
546	### Bot communication at the reviews
547	
548	Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
549	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
550	
551	- **At Work review**, summarize what changed and stop.
552	  "Work complete. Please review."
553	- **At Commit Description review**, present `$TITLE`
554	  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.
555	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
556	  --body ...` invocation by default.
557	- **At Post close-out review**, surface the shape
558	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;
559	  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
560	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
561	
562	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
563	
564	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
565	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
566	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
567	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
568	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
569	the next step seems obvious, wait.**
570	
571	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
572	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
573	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
574	  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
575	  turn's *final* push.
576	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
577	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
578	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
579	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
580	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
581	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
582	  user, after the turn, can capture it
583	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
584	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
585	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
586	  visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
587	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
588	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
589	  closing line after the push; that is a known slip.
590	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
591	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
592	  quiet, which flushes all bot session information into the
593	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
594	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
595	
596	### Recovery
597	
598	- **If push exits before its last stage** (`push-work`
599	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish (`squash-push-bot`)
600	  didn't run), run the squash+push by hand:
601	
602	  ```
603	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
604	  ```
605	
606	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
607	  exit, with no log file to chase.
608	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
609	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
610	  agents).
611	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
612	    command runs, so the invocation's own record plus any
613	    closing response land after the squash.
614	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
615	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
616	    change; it is not under the user's control.)
617	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
618	    `@` non-empty; e.g. the bot's back end may decide to
619	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
620	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
621	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
622	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
623	- **Nothing to clear after an out-of-band recovery.** Push
624	  keeps no saved state, so whatever you do to the repos by
625	  hand is simply the state the next run sees.
626	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
627	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
628	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
629	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
630	  push.
631	
632	## Iterative work
633	
634	When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
635	from incremental review, loop:
636	
637	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
638	2. Make the next round of changes.
639	3. User reviews the round (see
640	   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
641	4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
642	   new empty `@`.
643	5. If not done, go to step 2.
644	
645	Same jj mechanics as a
646	[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
647	single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.
648	
649	## Sub-cycle ladders
650	
651	When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
652	[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work
653	commits will live as a local jj `@` chain and
654	**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
655	parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
656	review and bisection only.
657	
658	### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder
659	
660	For each Work commit in the ladder:
661	
662	1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
663	2. Do the commit's work.
664	3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
665	   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
666	   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
667	   full suite, raising bisection cost.
668	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
669	   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
670	   into one final commit.
671	
672	**Nothing here is pushed.** The ladder is local until the
673	[Close-out squash](#close-out-squash-the-ladder), so no ladder
674	commit ever carries an `ochid:` trailer: the trailer is stamped
675	once, by `vc-x1 push`, on the squashed commit. Step 4 is
676	therefore first-time authoring of a scratch description, not a
677	rewrite of a published or stamped one, and is the named
678	exception to
679	[Re-describing](../AGENTS.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer).
680	
681	### Navigating the ladder
682	
683	Common moves:
684	
685	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
686	  from its base.
687	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
688	  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
689	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
690	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
691	  isolation.
692	
693	Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
694	descendants auto-rebase.
695	
696	### Close-out: squash the ladder
697	
698	When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:
699	
700	```
701	jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
702	```
703	
704	`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
705	keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
706	After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
707	intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.
708	
709	Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit. This is
710	the ladder's first and only publish, and where its `ochid:`
711	trailer is stamped. The scratch descriptions written at step 4
712	of the
713	[per-Work-commit contract](#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
714	never left the machine and never carried one, which is why
715	describing them freely is safe.
716	
717	For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
718	when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.
719	
720	### Recovery
721	
722	If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
723	prior commits:
724	
725	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
726	  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
727	  parent.
728	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
729	  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
730	  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
731	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
732	  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
733	  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
734	  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.
735	
736	# References
737	
738	- [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets): revset primitives
739	  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
740	- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
741	  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
742	  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
743	  bisection cost.
744
